title: The Rhetorical Analysis Essay
short: Organize by the writer’s strategies or by the text’s sections, with short quotations and commentary on each.
trouble: Learners organize by appeal (one paragraph each for ethos, pathos and logos) instead of following the writer’s moves.

blocks.html: With an analysis thesis in hand, the essay follows the writer’s moves. The most useful plans go through the text in order, or take one major strategy per section, always with short quotations and commentary.

blocks.name: wr-essay
blocks.cap: The map of a rhetorical analysis.

blocks.html: Organize by the writer’s strategies or the text’s sections, not by appeal. Each body paragraph names a move, quotes a few words of it, and explains its effect and purpose.

Writers don’t build speeches as one paragraph of ethos, one of pathos and one of logos; they build them as a sequence of moves. Following those moves lets you show how the parts work together and build, which is what makes an analysis convincing.

blocks.text: Plan for an essay on Douglass’s oration

items: Introduction: the situation (July 5, 1852; Rochester; an anti-slavery audience; a holiday celebrating liberty) and the thesis.
Move 1, the modest opening: “has stronger nerves than I have”; effect: goodwill and trust.
Move 2, the refusal to argue: “Must I argue the wrongfulness of slavery?”; effect: treats the answer as obvious, which makes any defense of slavery look absurd.
Move 3, the turn: “What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?”; effect: separates the speaker from the holiday and turns the celebration into an indictment.
Conclusion: how the moves build from trust to indictment.

blocks.html: Quote a few words, not whole paragraphs, and weave them into your sentences: Douglass asks his listeners what “your 4th of July” means to a slave. Then spend more words on commentary than on quotation.

blocks.title: One body paragraph
blocks.q: Write the topic sentence and commentary for Move 3 above.
steps: Topic sentence names the move and its job: Douglass finally separates himself from the celebration.
Quotation: he calls it “your 4th of July,” not ours.
Commentary: the pronoun shuts him out of the holiday, and the audience, who invited him to celebrate, must face why.
Tie to purpose: this prepares them for the indictment to come.
blocks.a: “Douglass finally separates himself from the holiday. By calling it ‘your 4th of July,’ he shuts himself out of the celebration his hosts invited him to join, forcing them to ask why a free man of their own town cannot share it, and preparing them for the indictment that follows.”

blocks.html: Organizing by appeal: one paragraph on ethos, one on pathos, one on logos. That plan breaks the text apart, repeats itself, and hides how the moves build. Check: do your body paragraphs follow the writer’s order or strategies? Could a reader rebuild the shape of the speech from your topic sentences?

blocks.name: wr-checklist

opts.title: Rhetorical analysis checklist
items: My introduction gives the situation: writer, audience, occasion, purpose.
My thesis names the purpose and the main strategies, and says how they serve it.
Each body paragraph follows a move or strategy in the text, not one appeal.
I quote short phrases and weave them into my sentences.
Every quotation is followed by commentary on its effect and purpose.
My conclusion shows how the moves work together.
